conflict_topics: kitchen smell affecting calls and laundry
dialogue_quality_notes: Exchange is concise and negotiative; participants propose concrete mitigations (weekend-only, fan, schedule, after-7).
Agents provide factual constraints (laundry days, work calls) that ground proposals.
No unnecessary repetition; proposals proceed logically from problem to trial mitigation to schedule/time compromise.
evaluation.final_reason: Parties reached a concrete, mutual schedule and time that address the main incompatible demands: Agent D agreed to limit cooking days and times ("Okay. So I'll cook on Tuesdays, Thursdays, or the weekend." then refined to "So, Tuesdays and Thursdays after 7."), Agent C accepted the days that avoid laundry nights ("Okay, that works."), and Agent A accepted the after-7 timing to protect work calls ("Yeah, after 7 is fine."). D adjusted cooking times/days in return for permission to continue cooking the dish; others accepted that adjustment.
position_change_notes: Agent D: initially defended the food as culturally significant ("It's devil curry... It's what I grew up with") but expressed willingness to avoid causing problems and later agreed to limit days and time ("Okay. So I'll cook on Tuesdays, Thursdays...", "I can cook after 7 p.m.").
Agent A: started by requesting no strong smells implicitly for work calls and moved to accept a concrete compromise (after-7 timing): "Yeah, after 7 is fine."

Agent C: moved from complaint (laundry picks up smell) to a specific scheduling request (avoid Mon/Wed/Fri) and accepted D's proposed days: "I do my laundry on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday... Can you cook it on the other days?" then "Okay, that works."
Agent B: offered a personal mitigation (closing door/open window) and did not insist on broader schedule changes; B's position remained largely consistent.

round_scores.evidence: Agent A: "...I'm on video calls for work right here until 7 p.m. The smell is a bit much." Agent B: "Yeah, my room is right next to the kitchen. The smell gets into everything." — multiple people report the smell as a problem, starting an incompatibility between cooking strong-smelling food and others' use of the flat.

Agent C: "My laundry is drying in the service yard. It picks up the smell." Agent D: "It's devil curry. It's what I grew up with. But I don't want to cause problems." — roles and stakes are clarified: D has a recurring cooking practice that causes the smell; others report concrete harms (laundry, rooms).

Agent A: "How about you cook it on the weekend?" Agent D: "The weekend could work. Agent B, Agent C, would that be any better for the smell... ?" — A offers a constraint and D expresses willingness to consider, reducing immediate hostility though not settled.

Agent B: "The day doesn't make a difference. The smell is the same." Agent D: "What if I open the kitchen window and use a fan... ?" — weekend proposal is contested; D proposes a mitigation but disagreement about whether timing solves the problem remains.

Agent A: "We can try it. But if the smell is still strong, can we just stick to cooking it on the weekend?" Agent D: "Okay, let's try the fan. But if that doesn't work, the weekend plan still leaves the same problem for Agent B and the laundry, doesn't it?" — parties agree to trial a mitigation while noting unresolved effects on others.

Agent A: "You're right, it doesn't." Agent B: "If I shut my door and open my window, the smell stays out of my room. It's fine." — partial technical mitigation for B reduces one person's stake, though laundry and living-room smell still contested.
Agent C: "Right, but that doesn't help the laundry." Agent B: "You're right." — agreement that B's mitigation doesn't solve C's problem; no new settlement.

Agent C: "A fan might just blow the smell into the service yard." Agent C: "I do my laundry on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday evenings. Can you cook it on the other days?" — C proposes a specific scheduling restriction to avoid laundry nights, sharpening the incompatibility into a concrete demand.

Agent D: "Okay. So I'll cook on Tuesdays, Thursdays, or the weekend. That works for me." Agent C: "Okay, that works. Thanks." — explicit agreement between D and C on days reduces the conflict over laundry scheduling, though other concerns (living-room smell during calls) remain unsettled.

Agent A: "But Tuesdays and Thursdays are still weekdays. The smell in the living room is the problem for my calls." Agent D: "Oh, right. I can cook after 7 p.m. on those days. Would that work?" — A raises remaining living-room/work concern; D offers a time adjustment as mitigation.

Agent A: "Yeah, after 7 is fine." Agent D: "Okay, great. So, Tuesdays and Thursdays after 7." — mutual, concrete acceptance of days and times resolves the substantive scheduling/timing conflict in speech-only terms.
No public speech or observable action recorded.

substantive_insights: Conflict combined temporal (when to cook) and spatial (smell reaching laundry and rooms) dimensions, requiring multiple mitigations.
Resolution combined a schedule (avoid C's laundry days) and a timing restriction (after 7) to protect A's calls — a layered compromise.
Technical mitigations (window/fan, closing door) partially solved individual impacts (B), but scheduling was needed for shared spaces (living room, service yard).
